statement: Python integrates user-defined objects with core language constructs — iteration, operator use, `len()`, subscripting, `with`-blocks — through special `dunder` methods such as `__len__`, `__getitem__`, and `__iter__`; you implement these methods and let the interpreter and built-in functions invoke them, rather than inventing ad-hoc method names.

The Python Language Reference warns that any use of `__dunder__` names that does not follow an explicitly documented use is subject to breakage without warning, so custom double-underscore names should be avoided.

`==` compares values (it is sugar for `a.__eq__(b)`) while `is` compares object identity; the only common correct use of `is` is testing against a singleton — chiefly `x is None` — and when unsure you should default to `==`.
condition: comparing a variable against a singleton such as None or a sentinel

statement: `list(x)` and the `x[:]` slice make a shallow copy: the outer container is duplicated but its elements are still shared references, which is fine for immutable items but means nested mutable items remain shared, so `copy.deepcopy` is needed when independent nested copies are required.
exception: every item held by the container is immutable

statement: A class that holds only fields with getters/setters and no significant behaviour is a code smell (`Data Class`): behaviour that manipulates the data tends to be scattered and duplicated across the system, so the responsibilities should usually be moved into the class.
exception: the class is deliberate scaffolding for a new module or an immutable intermediate representation crossing a boundary (e.g. JSON)

statement: A mutable object such as `[]` or `{}` must never be used as a parameter default value: the default is created once and shared by every call, so mutating it inside the function corrupts subsequent calls — use `None` as the default and build the object inside the function body.

List comprehensions and generator expressions build sequences more readably than `map`/`filter` or accumulation loops, but they can be abused; keep them short and side-effect-free, and when a comprehension runs to more than a couple of lines or exists only for its side effects, use an ordinary loop or a named generator function instead.
condition: the comprehension stays short and is free of side effects

statement: Use inheritance only when the object you are building is genuinely a specialized (is-a) version of its parent; when it merely uses another object as a component, prefer composition and delegation, which give looser coupling and hide the implementation detail.
condition: the new object merely uses another object as a component rather than being a specialized version of it

statement: Avoid subclassing built-in types such as `dict`, `list`, and `str`: their methods are implemented in C and bypass overridden dunder methods (for example `dict.update` ignores a redefined `__setitem__`), so the subclass only seems to work — use `collections.UserDict`/`UserList`/`UserString` or composition instead.

Python resolves attributes by dynamic binding (duck typing): code works with any object that provides the required attributes and methods regardless of its concrete type, so code should depend on the protocol an object supports, not on its class.

Python enforces no access control, so a single leading underscore (`_name`) is the convention that marks an attribute as internal and steers callers to the public interface; a double leading underscore (`__name`) triggers name-mangling and should be used only to prevent attribute clashes across an inheritance hierarchy.

Do not write explicit Java-style get/set methods; expose plain attributes and add a `@property` only when validation or a computed/read-only attribute is needed, which keeps a uniform attribute-access interface and avoids callers tracking which values need a trailing `()`.

Instances normally store attributes in a per-instance `__dict__`; for a class instantiated in large numbers with a fixed attribute set, defining `__slots__` replaces that dict with a compact array and substantially cuts memory, but it interacts badly with inheritance and removes `__dict__`, so it is a targeted optimization rather than a default.
exception: the class participates in inheritance or multiple inheritance, or other code relies on the instance `__dict__`

statement: Prefer the simplest construct that solves the problem — a plain class over metaclasses, descriptors, multiple inheritance, or mixins — because readability degrades as abstraction layers accumulate, and code that is hard to observe, debug, or test is itself a signal that the design should be reorganized.

Manage resources such as files, locks, and connections with the `with` statement / context managers rather than manual open/close, so cleanup runs automatically even when an error occurs and an explicit `close()` cannot be forgotten.

Do not catch an exception you cannot meaningfully handle where it occurs; if there is no sensible local recovery, let it propagate to a caller that can handle it instead of defensively checking every return value.
condition: there is no sensible way to recover from the failure at that location

statement: Keep `except` clauses as narrow as is reasonable; a blanket `except Exception` also swallows legitimate programming errors that should not be ignored and makes debugging difficult.
When raising errors yourself, define your own exception types (subclassing `Exception`) so that intentional application-level errors are distinguishable from genuine programming mistakes.
